newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX heat ends off amid bearish weather forecasts.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX heat ends off amid bearish weather forecasts.

text.p: NYMEX heating oil ended lower Tuesday amid forecasts for much above normal temperatures in the "heating oil belt" of the U.S. Northeast while heat stocks are more than ample at the tail end of the winter season.

"The weather is expected to be warmer here and for the rest of the world for that matter, and the warmer weather has been creating a surfeit," said Pat Hughes, market analyst with Chevron Corp in Walnut Creek, California.
March heating oil ended off 1.39 cents a gallon at 59.42 cents after falling to 58.50 cents, its lowest level in seven months.
Weather Services Corp said temperatures will run well above normal this week in the northeastern United States, the largest heating oil market in the world.

After that, the National Weather Service's six-to-10 day forecast starting February 23 called for normal temperatures in the region. But, as of February 7, the American Petroleum Institute (API) said heating oil stocks in the Northeast were about even with a year ago when the winter was colder.
Dealers said March crude bucked declines on short covering, settling up 11 cents a barrel at $22.52 while March gasoline ended off 0.09 cent a gallon at 64.16 cents.
Dealers noted small speculators had significantly increased short positions in crude according to the CFTC Futures Commitment of Traders Report as of February 11.
Local players took the opportunity to cover positions after an early session sell-off in the oil complex, dealers said.
"You had some covering before the expiry" said a New York crude trader. March crude expires at market's close Thursday.

Due to the U.S Presidents Day holiday Monday, the API will release weekly oil inventory data for the week ended February 14 on Wednesday after 1600 EST instead of at its usual time of Tuesday evening.
Preliminary estimates from traders called for a build in crude stocks of up to four million barrels due to relatively low operating rates by refiners.
Meanwhile, gasoline stocks were seen about steady as gasoline demand was expected to have recovered after falling to its lowest point in about two years the week before.

"You saw plenty of selling of heat for gasoline," said one dealer of Tuesday's action, noting gasoline was expected to remain strong relative to heating oil ahead of gasoline's traditional spring rally.
Gasoline typically rallys in the spring in anticipation of the summer driving season when gasoline demand usually peaks.
((-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761))
